name: Canon Griffin Rumanzi
bioShort: Canon Griffin Rumanzi (b. 1991, Uganda) is an artist working in digital photomontage and archival intervention. He combines archival images, colonial documents, family portraits and found photographs to examine Uganda's fragmented histories. He co-founded the public archive History in Progress Uganda (HIPUganda) with Andrea Stultiens. His solo exhibition Looking into the Mad Eye of History Without Blinking was shown at NCAI in 2025.
bioLong: Canon Griffin Rumanzi (b. 1991, Uganda) works with digital collage and archival material. Government seals, colonial papers, family portraits, anonymous snapshots and press images are cut, layered and recombined into photomontages that hold contradictory histories in a single frame. Works in the NCAI Collection, captioned in Luganda and English, draw on the late nineteenth-century history of the Buganda court, Christian missions and the execution of converts under Kabaka Mwanga.

His practice extends beyond the gallery through History in Progress Uganda (HIPUganda), a public archive co-founded with the artist and researcher Andrea Stultiens, which digitises and republishes photographs from or about Uganda's past. He has led workshops and collaborations with institutions including the Uganda Press Photo Award/FOTEA, Makerere University Library and Uganda Christian University.

Rumanzi has shown work at Fotomuseum Antwerp, Afriart Gallery Kampala, the Stellenbosch Triennale, Format Festival, Goethe-Zentrum Kampala and the Uganda National Museum, and has taken part in the Kampala Art Biennale, Addis Foto Fest, Noorderlicht Photo Festival and Nyege Nyege Festival. In 2018 he was in residence at 32° East | Ugandan Arts Trust.
His solo exhibition Looking into the Mad Eye of History Without Blinking, curated by Trevor Mukholi, was shown at NCAI from 11 September to 2 November 2025.

Several work titles have leading spaces and trailing \r\n in medium; all work years are blank (Art Africa dates one related work, 'Abaddu Working; We Are All Slaves', to 2020). name: Jak Katarikawe
nationality: Ugandan (lived and worked in Kenya from 1981)
bioShort: Jak Katarikawe (c. 1940–2018) was a Ugandan-born painter who lived and worked in Kenya from 1981. Largely self-taught, he developed a narrative, dreamlike figurative style drawn from village life, love and family. He was associated with Paa Ya Paa Arts Centre and Gallery Watatu in Nairobi. His work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili Na Roho and 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Jak Katarikawe was born around 1940 in Kigezi, southern Uganda. He received no formal art education; he cited as early influences his mother's paintings on the walls of the family home and the murals of the Catholic cathedral at Rushoroza. After years of casual labour, his talent was recognised by David Cook, a lecturer in literature at Makerere University in Kampala, who supported his early work.

Following Idi Amin's seizure of power, Katarikawe withdrew to his rural home in Kigezi, and in 1981 moved to Nairobi. He joined the newly established Paa Ya Paa Arts Centre and, from 1984, became one of the principal artists of Gallery Watatu. His paintings are narrative and personal, merging folklore, erotic fantasy and everyday village life; Western critics often called him the 'East African Chagall'. His technique moved from pencil and crayon to watercolour, wax crayon and occasional woodcuts, and later predominantly to oil.

The Museum of World Cultures in Frankfurt holds more than 150 of his works and in 2001 presented a touring exhibition spanning four decades of his career, accompanied by the monograph Bilder aus Träumen – Dreaming in Pictures by Johanna Agthe and Elsbeth Court. Katarikawe died in October 2018. His work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili Na Roho and in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Birth year uncertain: Red Hill gives c. 1940; MOMAA gives '1938 or 1940'. Death date 19 Oct 2018 from search snippets (kenyanartsreview, anotherglobaleater); Red Hill gives 1940–2018. DATA ERROR: several works have year values like '1939- 1997' / '(1939 - 1997)', which look like mis-entered life dates and do not match his dates. Medium 'Oil on Gouache' looks like an entry error. Sometimes recorded as 'Jak Moses Katarikawe' / 'Jack Katarikawe'.

name: Meek Gichugu
bioShort: Meek Gichugu (b. 1969, Ngecha, Kenya) is a painter associated with the Ngecha artists' community outside Nairobi. His surreal oil paintings combine strange animals, distorted figures, exotic fruit and sexual symbols in restrained ochre and earth tones. A sell-out solo show at Gallery Watatu in 1991 launched his career. His work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili Na Roho and 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Meek Gichugu was born in 1969 in Ngecha, on the outskirts of Nairobi. In the early 1990s Ngecha became known as the 'Village of Painters' after the founding of the Ngecha Artists' Association by Sane Wadu, Wanjiku 'Wanju' Brush and Chain Muhandi, and Gichugu began painting in that setting.

In 1991, at the age of 22, he was given a solo exhibition at Gallery Watatu in Nairobi, where most of the nearly 90 works on show were sold. His paintings depict a world in which the familiar and the sinister compete for space: exotic fruits, strange animals parading across the canvas, distorted human figures and hidden or overt sexual symbols. Working in oil on canvas, he favoured restrained mustard and ochre earth tones, later adding blues and reds as highlights; his Kenyan work changed little in style over the decade.

In 1999 Gichugu settled in Paris with his family, and his East African career came to an end; little has been published on his later work. Works in the NCAI Collection include Donkey Rider (1994) and Everything (1998). His work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili Na Roho and in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Birth year: Red Hill, MutualArt and Diawara & Schaffner give 1969; an Instagram post says 1968. CHECK DATA: 'Kalahari Desert' is dated 1969, the year he was born; probably a cataloguing error. Red Hill spells 'Wanju Brush'; I wrote 'Wanjiku "Wanju" Brush' as an expansion; revert to 'Wanju Brush' if unsure.

name: Kofi Dawson
bioShort: Galle Winston Kofi Dawson (1940–2021) was a Ghanaian modernist artist who worked across painting, drawing, printmaking, sculpture, text and installation. He trained at Kumasi and the Slade School of Fine Art, London, and was apprenticed to the engraver Amon Kotei. NCAI holds serigraphs, monoprints and a mezzotint from 1991 to 2016. His work was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025).
bioLong: Galle Winston Kofi Dawson was born in 1940, one of thirteen children of the architect Wilberforce David Kwami Dawson and Evelyn Esi Dawson. At Mawuli School in Ho he was taught art by Grace Kwami. He began a diploma in civil engineering at the Kumasi College of Technology before moving to fine art, and in 1964 joined the first cohort of three students on the BA Art (Painting) degree at what became the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology. A British Council award then took him to the Slade School of Fine Art in London, where he studied painting on canvas and screen printing.

Dawson was apprenticed to the Ghanaian modernist Amon Kotei, designer of the national coat of arms, who taught him engraving and colour separation at Victoriaburg Press. He worked for Ghana's Information Services Department and, after retiring in 2000, devoted himself to his practice. In 2009 he was the first artist to exhibit at the Nubuke Foundation in Accra (Nutata: drawings by GWK Dawson), and in 2019 the Savannah Centre for Contemporary Art in Tamale held a retrospective, curated by Bernard Akoi-Jackson.

Works in the NCAI Collection include the mezzotint Sankofa (2005) and the serigraph Eli Shaddai (2016). Dawson died in 2021. His work was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025), a collaboration between NCAI and SCCA Tamale.
notes: Non-East-African (Ghanaian). Full name Galle Winston Kofi Dawson (also 'G.W.K. Dawson'); consider using that as display name. Input 'exhibitions' is empty, but ncai254.com lists him in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (29 Apr–27 Jul 2025); link that in Sanity. Work title 'Suprano Choir' is probably a misspelling of 'Soprano Choir'; check against the work.

name: Paul Njihia
bioShort: Paul Njihia (b. 1991) is a self-taught Kenyan painter based in Nairobi. He began painting commissioned portraits in 2010 to support his studies, later working through Kuona Trust and from a studio at the Kobo Trust. His recent oil paintings, including Formation II and Same Old Story (2023), depict groups and parades. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection and Common Ground.
bioLong: Paul Njihia was born in 1991 and is a self-taught artist based in Nairobi. He began painting in 2010, producing commissioned portraits as a way to fund his education, and became a full-time artist after completing his studies.

In 2014 he became associated with the Kuona Trust Art Centre in Nairobi, and in 2017 he took a studio at the Kobo Trust. He has taken part in residencies in Konstanz, Germany (2015), through a Kenyan–German exchange, and at Nafasi Art Space in Dar es Salaam, and has shown his work in group exhibitions in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam.

The works by Njihia in the NCAI Collection are oil paintings made in 2022 and 2023, among them Checking the Results, Kindergarten Formation, Another Parade, Formation II and Same Old Story. Their titles point to scenes of assembly, ranking and ritual. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection and Common Ground.
notes: Birth year 1991 from Arak Collection only. Akka Project (search snippet) places him at 'Kobo Trust Studios'. Work title 'Kindergaten Formation' is misspelled in Sanity (should be 'Kindergarten'); I used the corrected spelling in the bio.

name: Boniface Maina
bioShort: Boniface Maina (b. 1987, Nanyuki, Kenya) works mainly in painting and drawing. His distorted, muscular figures, built from interwoven lines, explore the tensions of human interaction within physical and social space. He trained at the YMCA National Training Institute, Nairobi, and in 2013 co-founded the Brush Tu artists' collective. NCAI holds works from his 2020 series Old Realities.
bioLong: Boniface Maina was born in 1987 in Nanyuki, Kenya. He earned a diploma in Art and Design from the YMCA National Training Institute in Nairobi in 2008, and in 2013 co-founded Brush Tu, an artists' collective and communal studio in Nairobi.

Working predominantly in painting and drawing, Maina explores the inconsistencies and conflicts of human interaction within physical space. His exaggerated figures are drawn with interwoven lines that give them a muscular, anatomical appearance. Paint and ink are layered on different supports, and the backgrounds alternately deepen and limit the viewer's sense of space. The acrylic works on paper in the NCAI Collection, among them Minutes Past Curfew and works from the series Old Realities (2020), date from the period of pandemic restrictions.

His solo exhibitions include Line of Inquiry (The Art Space, Nairobi, 2016), Transitions (Nairobi Gallery, 2017) and Waiting, Watching and Wishing (Circle Art Gallery, 2020). Group exhibitions include Young Guns (Circle Art Gallery, 2017), East African Encounters (Cromwell Place, London, 2021), Walking the Edge (Afriart Gallery, Kampala, 2022), and Africa 1:1 (Ca' Pesaro, Venice, 2023), together with an Africa 1:1 Lab residency in Venice that year. He has shown at Art Dubai, Cape Town Art Fair and AKAA, Paris.
notes: Circle Art says he lives and works in Nanyuki; other sources (Strauss, Instagram) say Nairobi. I left current residence out. The link between the 2020 works and pandemic curfews is my reading of the titles and dates ('Minutes Past Curfew', 2020), not a sourced statement; remove if unwanted.

name: Josephine Alacu
bioShort: Josephine Alacu is a painter who worked in Kampala, Uganda, in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Her allegorical oil paintings, including Broken Eggs and The Legend (1980), use grotesque figures and religious imagery to address the violence of the Amin years and their aftermath. Her work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Josephine Alacu's paintings were made in Kampala in the late 1970s and early 1980s, a period of political violence in Uganda. Writing on modern art in Uganda, George Kyeyune places her work among the paintings made at the Makerere art school that criticised the Amin regime through veiled, allegorical messages.

In Broken Eggs (1980), Alacu draws on the biblical story of Genesis, filling the canvas with grotesques beneath an illuminated cross that hangs above a group of figures kneeling in prayer, which suggests that redemption from the torment of those years is possible. Mother's Nightmare offers a related image of the corrupt regime's effect on the national psyche. Both paintings are recorded in the Robert Loder Collection.

NCAI curator Don Handa has described the figurative paintings of Alacu and Peter Mulindwa, produced in Kampala in the early 1980s, as reflecting the training offered by the institution at the time and as allegories of Uganda's political and social conditions. Three oils on board by Alacu, Broken Eggs, Mother's Nightmare and The Legend, all dated 1980, are in the NCAI Collection. Her work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: No birth/death dates found. Nationality inferred from her work at the Makerere art school in Kampala (the sources do not state it outright). Pronoun 'her' is from the EAMAN text. DATE CONFLICT: EAMAN dates 'Mother's Nightmare' to 1978; Sanity has 1980. EAMAN credits Broken Eggs and Mother's Nightmare to the 'Robert Loder Collection'; check whether the NCAI works are the same objects (provenance).

name: Sebastian Kiarie
bioShort: Sebastian Kiarie (b. 1971) is a self-taught Kenyan painter who lives and works in Ngecha village outside Nairobi. His paintings, which he calls 'visual dialogues', question the values of the community he grew up in and the line between truth and myth. Works in the NCAI Collection include Mother and Child (1997) and A Couple (1993).
bioLong: Sebastian Kiarie was born in 1971 in Tanzania, where his extended family had settled to escape colonial reprisals during Kenya's 1950s State of Emergency. His parents returned to Kenya in 1976, and he grew up in Ngecha village, where the family dealt with land disputes and the stigma of being labelled 'deserters'.

He has said that the politically charged Kikuyu community of Ngecha led him early on to question the community's value systems, past and present. After finishing secondary school he began to respond to these questions through painting, creating what he calls 'visual dialogues' that blur the lines between truth and myth and between the personal and the collective. He is self-taught; his first exposure to painting came from the pictorial sign paintings of his surroundings.

Kiarie has held several solo exhibitions, including at Banana Hill Art Gallery, and has taken part in many group exhibitions. His work is in private and public collections in Kenya and abroad. He continues to live and work in Ngecha. The NCAI Collection holds A Couple (1993), acrylic on paper, and Mother and Child (1997), oil on canvas.
notes: Main source is an auction-house artist page (Veno.Art). Artsy and the Margaretta wa Gacheru blog were read only as search snippets (self-taught; sign paintings; Banana Hill show, Feb 2013).

name: Asaph Ng'ethe Macua
bioShort: Asaph Ng’ethe Macua (b. 1930, Karura, Kenya) is a painter who trained at Makerere in Kampala in the early 1950s and has been making art since the late 1940s. He later served as chief artist of the East African Common Services Organisation. His gouaches in the NCAI Collection span from Stone Mason (1964) to Mother and Child (1993). His work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili Na Roho.
bioLong: Asaph Ng’ethe Macua was born in 1930 in Karura, near Nairobi, and has been making art since the late 1940s. He attended Makerere in Kampala from 1951. After graduating he worked for the Department of Community Development in Kampala before returning to Kenya in 1958.

From 1960 he worked as chief artist for the East African Common Services Organisation, whose publishing work later passed to the Kenya Literature Bureau. Alongside this work he exhibited at Makerere University and the Uganda Museum in Kampala, at Chemchemi in Nairobi (1964), in Mankind and Nature at the Goethe-Institut, Nairobi (1992), and at the Alliance Française, Nairobi (1993). The National Museum in Nairobi held a retrospective in 2019, the same year he published his autobiography, From Misery to Joy: A Journey of Endurance.

The two gouaches on paper in the NCAI Collection, Stone Mason (1964) and Mother and Child (1993), span nearly three decades of his work. His work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili Na Roho, and he contributed to the accompanying catalogue, Mwili, Akili Na Roho / Body, Mind, and Spirit: Ten Figurative Painters from East Africa.
notes: Canonical name uses a curly apostrophe (Ng’ethe), as in the Mwili catalogue; Sanity uses a straight apostrophe, so use whichever house style prefers. Living status unconfirmed (no death record found). The publisher bio says he worked there 'until his retirement in 1967', which looks inconsistent, so I left the year out. A YouTube profile spells him 'Asapha'. The publisher text spells the venue 'Chemichemi'; the usual spelling is Chemchemi.

name: Florence Wangui
bioShort: Florence Wangui (b. 1986) is a Nairobi-born artist working in charcoal and oil. Trained first in zoology and biochemistry, she turned to art under the mentorship of Patrick Mukabi at the GoDown Arts Centre. Her introspective portraits and drawings of animals and figures carry a surreal, psychological charge. Her work was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025).
bioLong: Florence Wangui was born in Nairobi in 1986. She drew from an early age, and her drawings of the chickens and livestock around her home grew into the biological illustrations she made for school. That interest led her to study zoology and biochemistry, but her artistic career took over while she was training with the painter Patrick Mukabi at the GoDown Arts Centre. She later developed her oil-painting technique with the artist Dolores Gomez.

Wangui is known for detailed charcoal drawings on paper, including studies of hens, cocks and chicks, and for heavily textured oil portraits that show figures in trance-like or introspective states. Her work draws on expressionist portraiture and on symbolism, such as the recurring egg, to suggest the psychological defences that protect a vulnerable inner self. She has also made stained glass and bronze sculpture for sacred spaces.

She is represented by One Off Gallery in Nairobi. Her charcoal drawing Wait for It (undated) was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025), a collaboration between NCAI and SCCA Tamale. The NCAI Collection also holds the oil painting In A Moment.

name: Charles Mukasa
bioShort: Charles Mukasa is a Ugandan painter and a graduate of the Makerere art school in Kampala. He is represented in the NCAI Collection by Looting at Bombo (1979), an oil on board that responds to the violence and looting that accompanied the fall of Idi Amin's regime. The painting has been discussed in scholarship on art and politics in Uganda.
bioLong: Charles Mukasa is a Ugandan painter who graduated from the Makerere art school (now the Margaret Trowell School of Industrial and Fine Arts) in Kampala. Little biographical information about him has been published.

He is represented in the NCAI Collection by Looting at Bombo (1979), a large oil on board. Bombo, north of Kampala, was a major military garrison, and the painting's subject and date place it in the turbulent months around the end of Idi Amin's rule in 1979.

In his doctoral study Contemporary Art in Uganda: A Nexus between Art and Politics, Kizito Maria Kasule discusses the painting as an example of Ugandan artists responding directly to political events. He reads it as articulating the collusion between the soldiers of the period and the civilians who joined in the looting. A painting titled Looting at Bombo, oil on board and dated 1979, is also recorded in the catalogue of the Robert Loder Collection, credited to 'W Mukasa'.
Charles Mukasa should not be confused with the Ugandan painter Geoffrey Mukasa, who trained at Lucknow in India.
notes: Only facts: 'graduate of Makerere Art School' and the reading of the painting (search snippet of the Wits PhD thesis; I could not read the full 338-page PDF). VERIFY the thesis author's name (Kizito Maria Kasule) before publishing, or drop it. ATTRIBUTION CONFLICT: the Wits thesis says 'Charles Mukasa', 'Looting at Bombo (1980)'; the Loder Collection catalogue says 'W Mukasa', 1979, oil on board, 117 x 132, acquired 1993. The NCAI work may be the Loder object, so check provenance and the signature. The Bombo garrison and 1979 context sentence is general history, not from the sources; trim if strict sourcing is required. No dates found.

name: Seraphina Nshunju
bioShort: Seraphina Nshunju is a painter active in East Africa in the late 1960s. Their work was noted in a 1972 survey of contemporary artists in East Africa for its lyrical, surrealist treatment of female figures. Nshunju is represented in the NCAI Collection by Walking People (1968), an oil on canvas.
bioLong: Seraphina Nshunju was a painter active in East Africa in the late 1960s. Little biographical information about the artist has been published.

In 'Contemporary Artists in East Africa', a survey published in African Arts in 1972, J. D. Miller described how Nshunju 'achieves surrealist effects in a lyrical rendering of female figures on a pastel lawn, one trailing a peacock's tail, others with limbs fading into the grass.' The article discusses Nshunju alongside artists of the period such as the sculptor Francis Nnaggenda, which places the work in the circle of artists working in Uganda and the wider region at the time.

Nshunju is represented in the NCAI Collection by Walking People (1968), an oil on canvas. A work with the same title is also listed in the catalogue of the Robert Loder Collection. Walking People belongs to the period covered by the 1972 survey and gives a rare view of a practice that is otherwise little documented. Further research into Nshunju's training, exhibitions and later career is needed.
notes: Nationality, training and dates not found; nationality left null. Treat the 'Uganda and the wider region' context as an inference from the article's context (Nnaggenda), not a fact. The Loder catalogue lists 'Seraphina Nshunju, Walking People' under oil on board (search snippet), while Sanity has oil on canvas; check the medium. The journal's author 'J. D. Miller' and the date 1972 come from search-result metadata. I used they/them because the sources give no pronouns.

name: Kefa Frederick Sempangi
bioShort: Kefa Frederick Sempangi (b. 1939) is a Ugandan artist whose practice in the 1960s and 1970s spanned surrealist portraiture, abstract painting, found-object assemblage and cast bronze. He studied at Makerere's art school and the Royal College of Art, London, and later lectured at Makerere. He is represented in the NCAI Collection by Reptile (1967), an oil on board.
bioLong: Kefa Frederick Sempangi was born in Uganda in 1939. He studied fine art at the Margaret Trowell School of Fine Arts in Kampala and at the Royal College of Art in London, graduating in 1970, and later completed a PhD in art history at the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. On returning to Kampala he became a lecturer in art history at Makerere University. His work was exhibited in Uganda and the UK, including at the Camden Art Centre in London in 1968 and 1969.

In the 1960s and 1970s his practice spanned surrealist portraiture, abstract painting, found-object assemblage and cast bronze. His paintings often dealt with religion and morality and with internal conflict; he described his aim as capturing 'these hidden forces behind the natural, behind the superficial, behind the seen'. His sculpture Omugerengejjo, made of clay, cement, bone, animal skin and vegetable matter, sets Christian reference beside objects of divination.

In 1974 Sempangi and his family went into exile in the Netherlands and the United States, an experience recounted in his book A Distant Grief. On his return to Kampala in 1979 he founded what became the Presbyterian Church in Uganda, and he later served in public office while keeping up a personal art practice. His works are rare; the NCAI Collection holds Reptile (1967), an oil on board.
notes: Also spelled 'Ssempangi' (e.g. the 1998 catalogue 'Kefa Ssempangi Back to Art'). Living status unconfirmed (Strauss lists '1939–'). Strauss calls the church 'Presbyterian Church of Uganda'; the PCA history source says 'Presbyterian Church in Uganda'. The Loder Collection also lists a 'Kefa Sempangi – Reptile' (oil on board), so check provenance.

name: Ngugi Waweru
bioShort: Ngugi Waweru (b. 1987) is a self-taught Kenyan multimedia artist based in Nairobi and a co-founder of the Wajukuu Art Project in Mukuru. Working in woodcut, painting, sculpture and installation, he often transforms discarded materials. With Wajukuu he took part in documenta fifteen in 2022. His painting Talk to the Hand (2025) was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread.
bioLong: Ngugi Waweru was born in 1987 and grew up in Nairobi, where he lives and works. He is self-taught: he began making art after watching friends who had graduated from art college at work, and then committed to it full time. He works from the collective studio of the Wajukuu Art Project in Mukuru, one of Nairobi's largest informal settlements, which he co-founded with fellow artists and through which he mentors young people from the area.

His practice spans woodcut printmaking, mixed-media painting on canvas, sculpture and installation. He often transforms discarded materials into symbolic forms, addressing resilience, identity, environmental damage and the conditions of life in the settlement. His work is grounded in communal learning and collective ways of working.

In 2015 he was second runner-up in the Manjano art competition. As a member of Wajukuu he took part in documenta fifteen in Kassel in 2022, where one of his sculptures was acquired by the Neue Galerie, Kassel; the collective received the Arnold Bode Prize that year. In 2024 he presented Mbinguni Kume Pasuka at Circle Art Gallery, Nairobi. His painting Talk to the Hand (2025), acrylic and oil on canvas, was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025).
notes: BIRTHPLACE CONFLICT: Vantaart/Akka say born in Mukuru; an OnCurating snippet says born in Nakuru. I left the birthplace out. Input 'exhibitions' is empty, but ncai254.com lists him in Breaking Bread (2025); link it in Sanity. The Arnold Bode Prize went to the collective (Wajukuu), not to him alone.

name: Kelvin Haizel
bioShort: Kelvin Haizel is a Ghanaian artist working across photography, painting, video and archival intervention. His practice explores what he calls 'images about nothing', drawn from overlooked categories of objects. He studied at KNUST, Kumasi, where he is a PhD candidate. His video installation A Thing About Forevers (2016) was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025).
bioLong: Kelvin Haizel is a Ghanaian artist who works in various media, including photography, painting and archival intervention. He is interested in the speculative potential of what he terms 'images about nothing', images drawn from subcategories of objects. His practice combines personal inquiry with research into these kinds of objects, developing an aesthetic that inverts their social hierarchies. After a long break from painting he has returned to the medium with an abstract yet materialist and fictional visual language.

Haizel earned a BFA in Painting and Sculpture (2010) and an MFA (2018) from the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Kumasi, where he is a PhD candidate in the Department of Fine Art and Curatorial Practice. His solo exhibitions include Babysitting a Shark in a Cold Room: Comoros Encounters (Zurich, 2019), which won the A New Gaze 2 prize for contemporary photography, Archive of Experiences at the 8th Hamburg Photography Triennial, MARKK (2022), and We Do Not Sleep to Dream at Gallery 1957, Accra (2024).

Group exhibitions include Afrotopia at the Rencontres de Bamako (2017), the Stellenbosch Triennale (2020), ARoS Aarhus Kunstmuseum (2021) and the Museum of Contemporary Photography, Chicago (2022). A Thing About Forevers (2016), a video installation that reimagines the board game oware with pills in place of seeds, played in an endless loop with no winner, was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025).
notes: Non-East-African (Ghanaian). Birth year not found. The ncai254.com artist list misspells him 'Kevin Haizel' (the body text has 'Kelvin'), so fix it on the site. Input 'exhibitions' is empty; link Breaking Bread (2025) in Sanity. The oware/pills description comes from an NCAI X post (search snippet).

name: Eric Gyamfi
bioShort: Eric Gyamfi (b. 1990) is a Ghanaian photographer and artist whose process-driven practice extends the material and conceptual limits of photography. His 40-minute film Certain Winds from the South (2023), adapted from a short story by Ama Ata Aidoo, follows a young man's decision to migrate south. It was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025).
bioLong: Eric Gyamfi was born in Ghana in 1990 and lives and works there. He holds a BA in Information Studies with Economics from the University of Ghana (2014) and has pursued an MFA in the Department of Painting and Sculpture at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Kumasi. He was a fellow of the Photographers' Masterclass in Khartoum (2016), Nairobi (2017) and Johannesburg (2018), and took part in the Nuku Studio photography workshops and the World Press Photo West Africa masterclass in Accra.

His practice reworks conventional photography to explore time, transformation and identity. His work has been shown at the 11th and 12th Rencontres de Bamako (2017 and 2019), the Vienna Biennale (2021), FOAM and the Berlinale.

Certain Winds from the South (2023, 40 minutes) adapts Ama Ata Aidoo's short story of the same name. It follows Issah's decision to travel to the south of Ghana in search of a better life, told through an exchange between Issah and his mother-in-law, M'ma Asana, and traces a cycle of inequality that threatens their future. Shown as a video installation, the work was presented at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025), a collaboration between NCAI and SCCA Tamale.
notes: Non-East-African (Ghanaian). DATE CONFLICT: the ncai254.com Breaking Bread caption dates the film to 2012; UCSB and Sanity give 2023 (2023 is correct per UCSB), so fix the NCAI site caption. Input 'exhibitions' is empty; link Breaking Bread (2025) in Sanity.

name: Fabian Mpagi
bioShort: Fabian Mpagi (1953–2002) was a Ugandan painter known for his refined draughtsmanship and luminous colour. Drawing on Buganda fables, especially the creation myth of Kintu and Nnambi, he sought what he called 'the hidden values of spiritual abstraction'. He trained at Makerere, worked in exile in Kenya, and later directed Nommo Gallery in Kampala. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Fabian Mpagi graduated from the Margaret Trowell School of Industrial and Fine Art in Kampala in 1976 and returned there as a postgraduate student and teaching assistant. In 1983 he received a scholarship to study in Florence, Italy. On his return he went into political exile in Kenya, where he set up a studio and his career developed. He won the Habitat Art Competition in 1987, which brought a four-month residency in Paris.

In 1988 Mpagi returned to Uganda and soon became director of Nommo Gallery in Kampala, resigning in 1998 to concentrate on his own work. In 1992 he exhibited with Geoffrey Mukasa and Francis Nnaggenda in Uganda Modern Art at the Galerie am Stubentor in Vienna.

An astute draughtsman, Mpagi used rhythmic contrasts of colour to create a sense of shattered light and imaginative space. He was influenced by Buganda fables, especially the creation myth of Kintu and Nnambi. In a 1994 interview he explained: 'my interest was in the universal concerns of man – both pleasure and pain – so I studied the hidden values of spiritual abstraction.' After his death his work became widely scattered. The NCAI Collection holds an untitled portrait of the artist's mother and younger brother (1977), shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: DATE CONFLICT: Strauss/Circle Art give 1953–2002; the Wits PhD thesis says he 'died in 2001'; an Instagram auction post says born 1954. Using 1953–2002 (Circle/Strauss) for now; verify. The 1992 Vienna exhibition comes from the EAMAN bibliography (Ssengendo 1992 catalogue).

name: Beatrice Wanjiku
bioShort: Beatrice Wanjikũ (b. 1978, Ngong Hills, Kenya) is a Nairobi-based painter whose introspective work explores the psyche, identity and the tension between outside pressures and inner states. Her haunting, abstracted figures have moved through distinct phases since the early 2000s. She trained at the Buruburu Institute of Fine Arts. Her painting The Substance of Things (2025) was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread.
bioLong: Beatrice Wanjikũ was born in 1978 in the Ngong Hills area near Nairobi. After local primary and secondary schooling she studied at the Buruburu Institute of Fine Arts in Nairobi, graduating with a diploma in fine art in 2002, and has practised independently in Nairobi since then.

Her work is often described in distinct phases. A 'mortality' phase followed the death of her mother. In an 'X-ray' phase she appeared to strip away the exterior of her subjects. A phase drew on a three-month stay in Vermont that coincided with the Occupy Wall Street movement and incorporated newspaper clippings. A later introspective phase includes works such as The Strangeness of My Madness. Across these phases, her abstracted, often unsettling figures question social norms and internal conflict, drawing on her own experience and surroundings.

Wanjikũ has exhibited internationally, including, according to NCAI, at the Sharjah Triennial, the Venice Biennale and the Mercosul Biennial, and has held a number of fellowships and residencies. Her acrylic and mixed-media painting The Substance of Things (2025) was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025), a collaboration between NCAI and SCCA Tamale.
notes: Canonical spelling with tilde (Wanjikũ) follows Wikipedia; 'Wanjiku' without diacritic is also widely used. Input 'exhibitions' is empty, but ncai254.com lists her in Breaking Bread (2025); link it in Sanity. The biennial participation claims come from NCAI's own page and were not independently verified.

name: Sister Mary Nambi
bioShort: Sister Mary Nambi is an artist from Uganda represented in the NCAI Collection by Crested Crane and Snake Tree (1990), an oil on board. The crested crane in the title is Uganda's national emblem. Little biographical information about the artist has been published.
bioLong: Sister Mary Nambi is an artist from Uganda. Little biographical information about the artist has been published, and details of training, exhibitions and career have not been confirmed.

Nambi is represented in the NCAI Collection by Crested Crane and Snake Tree (1990), an oil on board. The grey crowned crane, the 'crested crane' of the title, is Uganda's national bird and appears on the country's flag and coat of arms, so the painting draws on an image closely tied to national identity. The pairing with a 'snake tree' suggests a scene drawn from the natural world and, possibly, from local narrative traditions, although no published interpretation of the work has been found.

A painting with the same title, Crested Crane & Snake Tree, oil on board, 142 x 99 cm and dated 1990, is recorded in the catalogue of the Robert Loder Collection, assembled by the British collector Robert Loder (1934–2017), a co-founder of the Triangle network of artists' workshops. That record lists the work's country as Uganda and its year of acquisition as 1993. Further research is needed into the artist's life and practice.
notes: Only source is the Loder Collection catalogue record (country Uganda, 1990, acquired 1993). 'Sister' suggests a member of a religious order, but this is unconfirmed, so I avoided pronouns. The crested crane as national emblem is general knowledge, not from the source; the 'possibly local narrative traditions' clause is interpretive, so cut it if strictness is needed. Possible Loder provenance for the NCAI work; check.

name: Charles Sekano
nationality: South African (lived in exile in Kenya, 1967–1998)
bioShort: Charles Sekano (1943–2024) was a South African painter, pianist and poet who spent some thirty years in exile in Nairobi, where he was known as 'Charlie in Exile'. He is best known for bold, multi-coloured pastel portraits of women. He exhibited with Gallery Watatu before returning to South Africa in 1998. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Charles Ezekiel Molefi Sekano was born on 18 November 1943 in Sophiatown, Johannesburg. He witnessed the forced removal of his community under apartheid, and his family was moved to Meadowlands in Soweto. At 21 he left South Africa, travelling through Botswana and Tanzania before being granted political asylum in Kenya in 1967.

In Nairobi, Sekano became a familiar figure in the city's art and music scenes, known as 'Charlie in Exile', and met other exiled southern African artists and activists at the National Theatre bar. He described his practice as the 'three Ps': painting, piano and poetry. His bold, multi-coloured pastel portraits of women began during the apartheid years, partly as a refusal to see faces only as black or white, and reflect a longing for home. He also made coiled-wire mobile sculptures, shown at the Goethe-Institut in Nairobi.

Sekano exhibited with Gallery Watatu during his years in Kenya and also showed widely in Germany. He returned to South Africa in 1998. From 2011 he was represented by the London dealer Ed Cross, and in 2015 he held his last major Kenyan exhibition at Red Hill Art Gallery, Nairobi. He died on 22 June 2024, aged 80. His untitled pastel on paper in the NCAI Collection was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Non-East-African by birth (South African), but lived in Kenya for about 30 years. AGE NOTE: born 18 Nov 1943 and died 22 Jun 2024 makes him 80, but African Contemporary and the Daily Nation headline say 'aged 81'. I wrote 80; check, or drop the age.

name: Ann Zziwa
bioShort: Ann Zziwa is an artist from Uganda represented in the NCAI Collection by Animal Life, an oil on board from the 1990s. Little biographical information about the artist has been published. A work of the same title, dated 1990, is recorded in the catalogue of the Robert Loder Collection.
bioLong: Ann Zziwa is an artist from Uganda. Little biographical information about the artist has been published, and details of training, exhibitions and career have not been confirmed.

Zziwa is represented in the NCAI Collection by Animal Life, an oil on board dated to the 1990s. As its title suggests, the painting takes animals and the natural world as its subject, a recurring theme in Ugandan painting of the period, alongside works in the collection such as Sister Mary Nambi's Crested Crane and Snake Tree (1990).

A painting recorded as Animal Life (Working Title), oil on board, 119 x 107 cm, is listed in the catalogue of the Robert Loder Collection, assembled by the British collector Robert Loder (1934–2017), a co-founder of the Triangle network of artists' workshops. That record gives the country as Uganda, the date as 1990 and the year of acquisition as 1993. The overlap in title, medium and period suggests a connection between the two records, which should be confirmed through further research into provenance. Further research is also needed into the artist's life and practice.
notes: Only source is the Loder Collection record (Uganda, 1990, acquired 1993; title 'Animal Life (Working Title)'). The Sanity date '1990's' should be standardised (Loder says 1990). Spelling may also appear as 'Anne Zziwa'. 'Recurring theme in Ugandan painting' is an editorial generalisation, so cut it if strictness is needed. I used no pronouns. Probable Loder provenance (like Nambi, Sempangi, Mukasa, Nshunju and Alacu works).

name: Francisco Goya
bioShort: Francisco de Goya (1746–1828) was a Spanish painter and printmaker. His etching series Los Desastres de la Guerra (The Disasters of War), made between 1810 and 1820 in response to the Peninsular War, departs from heroic battle imagery to show the suffering of soldiers and civilians. NCAI holds a copy of the series in book form, dated 1863, the year of its first publication.
bioLong: Francisco de Goya y Lucientes was born in 1746 in Fuendetodos, Spain, and died in 1828 in Bordeaux, France. One of the most important European artists of his time, he worked as a painter and printmaker.

Prompted by the Peninsular War between France and Spain (1808–1814), Goya made the etchings of Los Desastres de la Guerra between 1810 and 1820. The series departs from the tradition of patriotic and heroic battle scenes and shows the horror experienced by soldiers and civilians alike. It is arranged in three sections: scenes of war, scenes of the 1811–12 famine in Madrid, and the allegorical caprichos enfáticos (emphatic caprices). Goya gave each print a short, direct title that expresses his condemnation of the acts depicted.

The series was not published in Goya's lifetime. In 1863, thirty-five years after his death, the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando in Madrid published the first edition of 80 etchings, bound as a book, in a run of 500. The NCAI Collection holds a copy of Los Desastres de la Guerra dated 1863, a historical point of reference for the many modern and contemporary artists who have responded to war and political violence.
notes: NON-EAST-AFRICAN: Spanish old master. The item is a book (medium 'Book'), possibly a library or reference holding rather than an artwork. Confirm with NCAI whether it belongs in the artist index. The 1863 first-edition details (80 etchings, run of 500) are general facts about that edition; confirm the NCAI copy is a first edition rather than a later printing (editions followed in 1892, 1903, etc.). The Wellesley text counts '82 prints' for the full series, while the 1863 edition has 80. The closing link to East African artists responding to war is editorial framing; cut it if unwanted.
